stories.headline: Update: Western Europe Shatters Temperature Records for Second Consecutive Day as Heat Wave Kills Multiple People
stories.summary:
The United Kingdom recorded a temperature of 35.1 degrees Celsius (95.2 degrees Fahrenheit) at London's Kew Gardens on Tuesday, breaking the record of 34.8 C set just one day earlier at the same station and smashing a long-standing May benchmark of 32.8 C set in 1922. London also recorded a rare "tropical night" in which overnight temperatures never fell below 20 C. The heat wave has been described by the UK's Met Office as unprecedented in scope and timing for late May.

The extreme temperatures are driven by a "heat dome" — a high-pressure weather front trapping heat over Western Europe — which Météo-France says is producing conditions more than 10 degrees Celsius above seasonal averages. Records also fell in France, where temperatures reached 36 C in the country's southwest, and heat warnings were issued across Rome and other parts of the continent. Several drowning deaths were reported in Britain and France as people sought relief in rivers and open water.

Climate scientists emphasized that heat wave events of this intensity and unseasonable timing have been made significantly more likely and more severe by ongoing climate change. The UK government issued warnings about risks to life, particularly for elderly and vulnerable populations. Authorities urged residents to stay hydrated, avoid direct sun during peak afternoon hours, and check on at-risk neighbors.

The heat wave is the same system previously reported in South Asia, which has now extended its reach into Western Europe earlier in the year than climatologists typically observe. Meteorologists warned that the dome could persist for several more days before a cooler Atlantic weather system brings relief to northwestern Europe.

stories.headline: Measles Kills More Than 500 Children in Bangladesh as Cases Surpass 60,000
stories.summary:
More than 500 children with suspected and confirmed measles cases have died in Bangladesh since March, according to the country's health ministry, as the number of suspected infections has surpassed 60,000 in just over two months. Hospitals across the country are overwhelmed, with families of sick children reporting being turned away or unable to find beds. UNICEF confirmed its staff have been deployed to help hospitals triage and isolate incoming patients where such measures are lacking.

The outbreak has been exacerbated by vaccination gaps, supply shortages, and delays in diagnosis. One father described taking his daughter to receive the measles vaccine four times — twice she was turned away because she had a cold, and twice the vaccine was said to be unavailable — before she contracted the disease, was hospitalized repeatedly, and died after 27 days on life support at age four. Doctors and nurses have had Eid holiday leave cancelled as the government runs an emergency mass vaccination campaign.

Measles is highly contagious, spreading through respiratory droplets, and is especially dangerous for unvaccinated children under five. Public health experts note that poor healthcare infrastructure and long delays in seeking treatment, particularly among lower-income populations who avoid hospitals until conditions are critical, have contributed to the high death toll. Laboratory confirmation of the full case count is still pending.

The scale of the Bangladesh outbreak adds to a global pattern of measles resurgence driven by pandemic-era disruptions to routine childhood vaccination. UNICEF and the World Health Organization have both flagged measles as one of the top vaccine-preventable disease threats in low- and middle-income countries, citing declining immunization coverage in the years following COVID-19.

stories.headline: South Carolina Senate Defies Trump, Rejects Mid-Decade Congressional Redistricting
stories.summary:
The South Carolina state Senate voted 26-18 Tuesday to reject a mid-decade congressional redistricting effort backed by President Donald Trump, ending the administration's push to redraw maps that would have split the district of Rep. Jim Clyburn, the state's only Democratic congressman and a prominent figure in national Democratic politics. The vote came during a special legislative session and marks a notable instance of Republican state lawmakers directly defying Trump's political objectives.

Trump had pressured South Carolina's Republican-dominated legislature to redraw district lines ahead of the November midterms, part of a broader nationwide effort by his administration to manufacture additional Republican-friendly seats in Congress. The redistricting push has met mixed results: a Florida judge on the same day blocked a legal challenge to a new GOP-favored House map in that state, while a separate federal three-judge panel blocked Alabama from implementing a new congressional map it found was drawn with intentional racial discrimination against Black voters.

Proponents of mid-decade redistricting, including Trump and House Republican leadership, argue the moves are a legitimate and necessary response to Democratic-drawn maps elsewhere and a tool to preserve the GOP's narrow House majority through the 2026 elections. Opponents — including some Republicans who voted against the measure in South Carolina — counter that rapid, politically motivated remapping undermines voter trust, is legally vulnerable, and that with early voting already underway in some states, the timing is logistically untenable.

The outcome in South Carolina is seen as a significant setback for the White House's pre-midterm map strategy, and it adds to a patchwork of federal court rulings and state legislative decisions that have complicated Republican redistricting efforts across the South. The Alabama ruling is expected to be appealed to the Supreme Court.

stories.headline: NASA Unveils Contracts and Timeline for Permanent Moon Base
stories.summary:
NASA on Tuesday announced contracts with Blue Origin, Intuitive Machines, and Astrobotic to build robotic landers, hopping drones, and surface vehicles as the first phase of its Ignition Moon Base program. The agency aims to send 25 robotic launches and deliver four metric tonnes of cargo to the lunar south pole by 2029, with human habitation in semi-permanent housing targeted by 2032. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said the announcements mean the U.S. will 'never give up the Moon again.'

The program is unfolding against a backdrop of direct competition with China, which is pursuing its own crewed lunar landing by 2030. China on Monday launched its Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, keeping pressure on NASA to demonstrate momentum. Some independent scientists told BBC News they would not be surprised if China lands humans on the Moon before the United States, citing NASA's ongoing difficulties securing a human-rated lunar lander.

The Moon's south pole is the primary target because of water ice deposits that could support long-term habitation and fuel production for future Mars missions. The three-phase plan calls for robotic exploration first, followed by nuclear and solar power infrastructure, and finally crewed semi-permanent settlement. Most outside experts consider NASA's 2032 timeline highly ambitious given current program challenges.

The announcement represents a significant milestone in the Trump administration's space policy, which has emphasized lunar return before the president leaves office in 2028. The $20 billion program, unveiled in March, now has named contractors and a phased mission schedule, giving the effort more concrete shape than previous planning documents.

stories.headline: DOE Selects Five Companies for Negotiations Over Use of Surplus Weapons-Grade Plutonium as Reactor Fuel
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of Energy has selected five companies for advanced negotiations over the potential allocation of surplus plutonium — historically used in nuclear warheads — as fuel for commercial nuclear power reactors. A DOE spokesperson confirmed Tuesday that roughly 20 tonnes of Cold War-era material from dismantled weapons could be made available to the firms. The agency said the move could address a shortage of nuclear fuel while providing an alternative disposal pathway for the stockpile.

Proponents, including the companies involved, argue that converting the weapons-grade material into mixed-oxide or other reactor fuel is a safer and more economical method of disposal than burial, while also contributing to U.S. energy supply. The surplus plutonium has long posed a storage and nonproliferation challenge for the federal government, and previous disposal efforts have faced significant cost overruns.

The proposal has drawn criticism from nuclear nonproliferation experts, who warn that expanding commercial use of weapons-grade plutonium increases the risk of diversion and complicates international arms control norms. Critics argue that the material should be immobilized and permanently disposed of rather than cycled back into an energy supply chain with a broader set of handlers.

The decision comes as the Trump administration has pushed to expand domestic nuclear energy capacity and reduce dependence on foreign uranium supplies. If negotiations result in contracts, the move would represent one of the most significant repurposings of U.S. nuclear weapons material in decades.

stories.headline: South African President Ramaphosa Files Legal Challenge to Block Impeachment Proceedings
stories.summary:
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa filed a legal challenge Tuesday at the Cape Town High Court seeking to set aside a parliamentary panel report that has paved the way for impeachment proceedings against him. The challenge targets a report from an independent panel that found Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct related to the theft of $580,000 in cash hidden in a sofa at his private Phala Phala farm, a scandal local media have dubbed 'Farmgate.' Ramaphosa argued in his submission that the panel 'misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted' the charges against him.

The impeachment process was reopened after a Constitutional Court ruling earlier this month found that parliament had acted unconstitutionally in 2022 when it voted against establishing an inquiry — a vote that succeeded because Ramaphosa's ANC party then held a parliamentary majority. Since losing that majority in the 2024 general election, the ANC governs as part of a coalition, leaving Ramaphosa more politically exposed.

Parliament's Speaker has already formed a 31-member impeachment committee drawn from 16 political parties to consider whether grounds exist to proceed. The committee includes nine ANC members, meaning Ramaphosa cannot rely on party loyalty alone to shield him from the process. If the inquiry proceeds and parliament votes to impeach, it would be the first such removal of a South African president since the end of apartheid.

Ramaphosa has consistently denied wrongdoing, maintaining the cash found at the farm was proceeds from the legitimate sale of buffalo. The legal challenge, if successful, would annul the committee's mandate before it begins its work. The High Court hearing is expected to determine whether the impeachment process can continue while the legal challenge is pending.

stories.headline: Australia Confirms First Diphtheria Death in Nearly a Decade Amid Worst Outbreak Since 1991
stories.summary:
Australia's Northern Territory confirmed Tuesday that a man who died in April at Royal Darwin Hospital was killed by diphtheria, the country's first diphtheria death since 2018. Autopsy results from an overseas laboratory confirmed the cause of death, NT Health Minister Steve Edgington announced. The death comes as Australia grapples with its worst diphtheria outbreak in more than three decades, with 245 cases recorded this year, concentrated largely in remote Indigenous communities.

The outbreak was declared in March and has spread across the Northern Territory, Western Australia, South Australia, and Queensland. Cases began rising in late 2025 with a sharp acceleration in February. Sixty percent of this year's cases are in the Northern Territory, with Western Australia accounting for roughly 36 percent — including the first respiratory diphtheria cases recorded in that state in more than 50 years.

Australia's Chief Medical Officer declared diphtheria a communicable disease incident of national significance last week, and the government announced a AU$7.2 million package to boost vaccinations and resources in affected areas. Since late March, more than 10,400 vaccinations have been administered, and health officials said Tuesday that the number of new cases is now falling. Pop-up vaccination clinics have been established in Darwin, Katherine, and Alice Springs.

Diphtheria is a bacterial infection preventable by vaccine, typically administered in a series of five doses in childhood with a booster in early adolescence. Respiratory diphtheria can cause severe throat swelling, breathing difficulties, and death. Health authorities are urging teenagers and adults in affected communities to obtain booster shots, warning that gaps in vaccination coverage — particularly in remote areas — have driven the outbreak.

stories.headline: Federal Court Blocks Alabama GOP Redistricting Map, Citing Intentional Racial Discrimination
stories.summary:
A three-judge federal panel unanimously blocked Alabama from using a Republican-drawn congressional map in the 2026 midterm elections, ruling Tuesday that the lines were drawn to intentionally discriminate against Black voters in violation of the Constitution. The panel wrote it could not require Alabamians to vote under a map "tainted by intentional race-based discrimination," ordering the state to revert to a prior configuration that preserves two majority-Black districts.

The blocked map had been passed by the Republican-controlled state legislature in 2023 but never went into effect after the same court previously found it was drawn with discriminatory intent. The ruling comes amid a broader national debate over mid-decade redistricting efforts pushed by President Trump and his allies in several states, including South Carolina, where the Republican-led Senate voted Tuesday to kill a similar redistricting push 24-20.

Alabama is widely expected to appeal the decision, and the case could ultimately reach the Supreme Court ahead of November's midterms. Republicans have argued the maps reflect legitimate political line-drawing, while Democrats and civil rights advocates contend the efforts are designed to dilute Black voting power and entrench GOP majorities.

The ruling is one of the most significant federal court interventions in the 2026 redistricting cycle and carries implications for the balance of power in the U.S. House, where Democrats are competing to regain a majority.

stories.headline: Trump Administration Proposes Government-Wide NDAs for Federal Workers to Curb Leaks
stories.summary:
The Office of Personnel Management released a draft nondisclosure agreement Tuesday that would require all current and future federal employees to sign legally binding pledges not to share confidential government information with journalists or unauthorized parties. The Trump administration cited a series of high-profile unauthorized leaks as justification for the sweeping measure.

The proposal marks a significant expansion of information controls across the federal workforce and comes amid the administration's broader crackdown on perceived disloyalty within government agencies. Critics warn the NDAs could have a chilling effect on whistleblowing and the free flow of information to the public and Congress, while administration supporters say protecting sensitive government deliberations is a legitimate security interest.

The draft is open to agency adoption and does not yet carry the force of law, but its release signals the White House intends to push the policy across departments. Civil liberties groups and press freedom organizations are expected to challenge the proposal.

The move adds to a series of actions the administration has taken to tighten control over government communications, including personnel changes at federal agencies and the recent removal of Justice Department press releases related to January 6 prosecutions.

stories.headline: BP Ousts Board Chairman Albert Manifold Over Governance and Conduct Concerns
stories.summary:
BP removed board chairman Albert Manifold on Tuesday, citing "serious concerns" related to "important governance standards, oversight and conduct." The company did not elaborate on the specific nature of the concerns, and Manifold had only been in the role since October 2025.

The dismissal marks the second major leadership departure at BP in six months. New CEO Meg O'Neill was appointed in December following the surprise resignation of Murray Auchincloss after roughly two years leading the company. The back-to-back exits at the top represent deepening instability at BP as it navigates a strategic pivot away from fossil fuels and manages investor pressure over its direction.

BP shares fell more than 4 percent in both U.S. and UK markets following the announcement, reflecting investor anxiety about the company's direction and governance. BP is already under scrutiny for its financial performance and has faced calls from activist shareholders for a more decisive strategy.

The loss of both its chief executive and board chairman in rapid succession is highly unusual for a major publicly traded company and raises questions about internal culture and boardroom dynamics at one of the world's largest energy firms.

stories.headline: Update: DR Congo Ebola Governor Warns of Catastrophe as Case Count Tops 900; Funding Gap Looms
stories.summary:
The military governor of DR Congo's Ituri province, the epicenter of the current Ebola outbreak, issued an urgent warning Tuesday that his region is at risk of "descending into catastrophe" without a swift influx of resources. Governor Johnny Luboya Nkashama told French broadcaster RFI that affected communities lack adequate food, qualified medical personnel, and secure treatment centers, comparing the fight against the virus to a war the province is not equipped to wage.

Officials now report more than 900 suspected cases and 223 suspected deaths since the outbreak was declared on May 15. The World Health Organization has declared a public health emergency of international concern and warned the disease may be spreading faster than originally estimated, with cases confirmed in DR Congo's North and South Kivu provinces and seven confirmed cases in neighboring Uganda.

Africa CDC Director-General Dr. Jean Kaseya said regional health ministers have agreed on a $319 million response budget, but only about 10 percent of that sum has been secured so far. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa pledged an initial $5 million on Monday, and African business leaders are expected to convene later this week to raise additional funds.

The outbreak is compounding a dire humanitarian situation in Ituri, which has been under military rule since 2021 due to the presence of dozens of armed groups, including an affiliate of the Islamic State. Aid organizations have previously warned that the combination of active conflict and disease is severely hampering the response.

stories.headline: Update: Russia Threatens Systematic New Strikes on Kyiv, Orders Foreign Nationals to Leave
stories.summary:
Russia's Foreign Ministry on Tuesday threatened a fresh wave of 'systematic strikes' on Kyiv targeting 'decision-making centres, command posts, and drone manufacturing facilities,' and called on foreign nationals and diplomats to leave the Ukrainian capital as soon as possible. The warning came days after one of the largest Russian aerial assaults of the war, which killed four and injured approximately 100 people over the weekend using dozens of ballistic and cruise missiles, hundreds of drones, and a nuclear-capable Oreshnik hypersonic missile near Bila Tserkva, south of the capital.

The weekend strikes destroyed or damaged the Chernobyl Museum, the National Art Museum of Ukraine, a shopping center, a market, and several residential buildings. Russia framed the attacks as retaliation for a Ukrainian strike on a dormitory in Russian-occupied Starobilsk, which Moscow says killed 21 people. Ukraine's military said it had targeted an elite Russian drone unit in the area and did not strike civilians.

Ukraine characterized Russia's evacuation warning as 'shameless blackmail,' saying Moscow was 'effectively admitting that its shelling is aimed, among other things, at intimidating the foreign diplomatic corps.' Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov separately urged U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to evacuate American diplomats from Kyiv. The escalation comes after a brief ceasefire tied to Russia's Victory Day parade in May expired, since which multiple deadly strike waves have hit the capital.

The explicit public threat to escalate targeting in Kyiv, combined with instructions for diplomats to leave, marks a significant rhetorical and strategic escalation. Analysts note that such warnings are designed both to pressure Ukraine's allies and to justify planned military action, raising concerns among NATO members about the trajectory of the conflict.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Says U.S. Deal 'Not Imminent' Despite Progress; Republican Hawks Press Trump to Hold Firm
stories.summary:
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baqai said Tuesday that while negotiators have reached conclusions on 'a large portion of the issues under discussion,' a formal agreement with the United States is not imminent. The statement tempered optimism expressed over the weekend by President Trump, who had suggested a deal was close, and by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said Monday in New Delhi that an announcement had been expected 'last night' or 'today.' Rubio cautioned against reading too much into the delay.

U.S. intelligence reportedly believes Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei — who was injured in an Israeli strike at the outset of the war that also killed his father and predecessor — is in an undisclosed location, complicating communications with Iranian envoys and slowing the pace of talks. The reported framework under discussion involves a 60-day ceasefire extension, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz (through which 20 percent of global oil and liquefied natural gas passes), and a roadmap for further negotiations on Iran's nuclear program. Key issues including the scope of sanctions relief, release of frozen Iranian assets, and limits on Iran's nuclear activities remain unresolved.

The prospective deal has drawn sharp criticism from within Trump's own party. Sen. Ted Cruz called it 'a disastrous mistake,' Senate Armed Services Committee chairman Roger Wicker warned that a 60-day ceasefire would squander gains from 'Operation Epic Fury,' and close Trump ally Sen. Lindsey Graham questioned whether the war's objectives had been achieved. Trump dismissed his critics as 'losers,' saying any deal would be 'a great and meaningful one, or there will be no deal.'

Oil prices fell and Asian markets rose on Monday in anticipation of a potential agreement, reflecting the global economic stakes. Even if a deal is reached, shipping industry officials cautioned it could take months before supply chains through the strait return to normal. The standoff underscores the complexity of ending the conflict and the domestic political constraints on both sides.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Strikes Iranian Vessels and Missile Sites as Iran Warns American Bases No Longer Safe
stories.summary:
The U.S. military carried out fresh strikes in southern Iran on Tuesday, targeting Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps boats attempting to lay mines in the Persian Gulf and missile launch sites, even as peace negotiations continued in Doha. U.S. Central Command described the strikes as defensive actions taken to protect American forces. Iran's Foreign Ministry accused the U.S. of a "grave violation" of the April 8 ceasefire and said the strikes were a hostile act. Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned that U.S. military bases in the Middle East would "no longer be safe" after the war.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that finalizing a peace framework could take "a few more days," walking back President Trump's weekend suggestion that a deal was imminent. Iran's chief negotiator cited "frequent changes" in American positions and Israeli interference as key obstacles. The emerging framework under discussion would include a 60-day ceasefire extension, a halt to fighting on all fronts, and a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz while nuclear talks proceed separately.

The strikes represent the most significant escalation since the ceasefire took effect and have injected new uncertainty into the most advanced diplomatic push yet to end the nearly three-month conflict. Oil markets, which had priced in a deal-driven supply surge, pulled back on the news. Former National Security Adviser John Bolton publicly said the ceasefire and negotiations are "a mistake" and expressed hope the talks would collapse, reflecting continued hawkish opposition within Republican circles.

Israel separately announced it would intensify strikes on Hezbollah in Lebanon, with Prime Minister Netanyahu vowing to "crush" the group despite a recently extended ceasefire. The Quad nations — the U.S., Japan, India, and Australia — launched a new maritime surveillance initiative for the Indo-Pacific at their New Delhi summit, partly in response to the Hormuz crisis. The confluence of military strikes, stalled diplomacy, and regional escalation makes this the most consequential developing story of the day.

stories.headline: Texas Senate Runoff Pits Trump-Backed Ken Paxton Against Incumbent John Cornyn
stories.summary:
Texas voters headed to the polls Tuesday in a Republican Senate primary runoff that has become the latest high-stakes test of President Trump's ability to oust incumbent members of his own party. Trump endorsed state Attorney General Ken Paxton last week, setting up a confrontation with Sen. John Cornyn, a four-term incumbent and former Senate Majority Whip. The race has drawn roughly $100 million in spending and is among the most expensive Senate primaries on record.

Paxton, who survived a 2023 impeachment trial in the Texas Senate and faces a separate federal securities fraud indictment, has positioned himself as a Trump loyalist fighting GOP "establishment" figures. Cornyn, who has a reliably conservative voting record, has argued he is more effective at delivering results for Texas and better positioned to hold the seat in November. Both campaigns have run ads targeting the state's Muslim community, drawing criticism for what observers called inflammatory appeals.

Republican strategists warn that a Paxton victory could drain national party resources in a state that should be safely Republican, diverting money from competitive races elsewhere. Democrats are watching closely, viewing a Paxton nomination as an opportunity to compete in Texas in November. The race also fits a pattern: Trump has already helped defeat Rep. Thomas Massie in Kentucky and Sen. Bill Cassidy in Louisiana.

The outcome will signal how much influence Trump retains in Republican primaries heading into the 2026 midterms, where the GOP is defending a narrow House majority and several vulnerable Senate seats. Analysts note that Trump's power is strongest in closed Republican primaries in red states, but that primary victories do not automatically translate into general election strength in competitive districts and states.

stories.headline: Four Killed, Including Two Children, as Train Hits School Minibus at Belgian Level Crossing
stories.summary:
A passenger train struck a school minibus at a level crossing in Buggenhout, northern Belgium, on Tuesday morning, killing two children aged 12 and 15 and two adults — the driver and a chaperone. Five other children on the bus were hospitalized in critical but stable condition. The bus was transporting seven children to a special education school when the collision occurred shortly after 8 a.m. local time.

Belgian federal police and rail officials confirmed that the level crossing barriers were already down and warning lights active when the minibus driver turned onto the tracks. The train was traveling at approximately 90 kilometers per hour on approach to Buggenhout station and struck the minibus with extreme force, throwing it into the driveway of a nearby house. No passengers on the train were injured, though one person was treated for shock.

Belgian mobility minister Jean-Luc Crucke and Flemish education minister Zuhal Demir both expressed condolences, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "Europe grieves with Belgium." An investigation has been launched by police and the public prosecutor's office into how the accident occurred despite active safety barriers.

The crash is the deadliest rail crossing accident in Belgium in recent years and prompted immediate calls for review of level crossing safety protocols. Rail operator Infrabel said CCTV footage confirms the barriers and signals were functioning correctly at the time of the crash.

stories.headline: Georgia and Pennsylvania Primaries Produce Key Senate and Governor Runoffs
stories.summary:
Georgia held its 2026 primary elections Tuesday, with multiple major races heading to June runoffs. In the Republican gubernatorial primary, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones and billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson advanced to a June 16 runoff, while Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger was eliminated. On the Democratic side, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the gubernatorial nomination outright.

In the Republican U.S. Senate primary, Rep. Mike Collins and former University of Tennessee football coach Derek Dooley — backed heavily by Gov. Brian Kemp — advanced to a runoff, with Dooley edging out Rep. Buddy Carter for the second spot. In Pennsylvania, union leader Bob Brooks won the Democratic Senate primary with endorsements from Sen. Bernie Sanders and Gov. Josh Shapiro.

The Georgia results carry significant national implications heading into the 2026 midterms. Democrats view the governor's race as a potential pickup opportunity in a state President Biden narrowly carried in 2020, while Republicans are working to consolidate their Senate majority. The Kemp-backed Dooley's strong showing signals the governor's continued influence in state GOP politics despite tensions with Trump allies.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Launches New Strikes on Iran Near Bandar Abbas; Deal Still Possible, Rubio Says
stories.summary:
U.S. Central Command announced Monday it conducted new strikes in southern Iran near Bandar Abbas, targeting Iranian missile sites and boats allegedly attempting to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The strikes were characterized as defensive, designed to "protect our troops from threats posed by Iranian forces" while a ceasefire remains nominally in place. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it downed a U.S. drone and fired on a fighter jet and another drone that it claimed entered Iranian airspace.

Despite the escalation, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a diplomatic deal remains possible, describing ongoing talks over specific language in an initial agreement framework. The reported deal would involve a 60-day ceasefire extension, reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and a framework for further nuclear negotiations — though Iran's foreign ministry said Monday that a signing is "not imminent." Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, reportedly sheltering in an undisclosed location after being wounded in an earlier Israeli strike, has been cited by U.S. intelligence as a complicating factor in the pace of talks.

The potential deal has fractured Republican unity, with Senators Ted Cruz, Roger Wicker, and Lindsey Graham publicly warning it would be too lenient on Iran. Trump dismissed his critics as "losers," saying the deal would be "great and meaningful" or there would be no deal at all. Oil prices fell and Asian markets rose Monday on hopes of an agreement, underscoring the economic stakes tied to the Strait of Hormuz, through which approximately 20 percent of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas passes.

stories.headline: Update: Ebola Death Toll Reaches 220 as WHO Warns Outbreak Is Outpacing Response
stories.summary:
The World Health Organization announced Monday that at least 220 people have died in the ongoing Ebola outbreak centered in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with suspected cases now surpassing 900. WHO director-general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warned that the outbreak is outpacing response efforts, a significant escalation from previous assessments. Health workers are operating screening checkpoints between villages in the eastern Ituri province, where the outbreak is believed to have originated.

The outbreak has already spread beyond Congo's borders, with Uganda reporting new confirmed cases in recent days. Aid organizations have described a massive logistical crisis in reaching affected communities in the remote eastern DRC. The WHO had previously raised the risk level to "very high" as Red Cross volunteers were reported among the dead.

Ebola carries a high fatality rate and spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals. An outbreak surpassing 900 suspected cases with deaths now at 220 represents a serious and accelerating public health emergency with potential regional implications across Central and East Africa.

stories.headline: Jazz Legend Sonny Rollins, 'Saxophone Colossus,' Dies at 95
stories.summary:
Sonny Rollins, widely regarded as one of the greatest jazz musicians in history, died Monday at his home in Woodstock, New York, at the age of 95. His publicist described him as "one of the most honored and influential figures in American music." The cause of death was not announced; respiratory illness had forced Rollins to retire from performing in 2014.

Born Walter Theodore Rollins in New York City in 1930, he began playing saxophone at age seven and rose to prominence in the late 1940s and 1950s, collaborating with Miles Davis, Charlie Parker, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk, Art Blakey, and Bud Powell. His 1956 album Saxophone Colossus became one of the defining records in jazz history, and his 1962 album The Bridge was inspired by his legendary practice sessions on New York's Williamsburg Bridge. He won two Grammy Awards and received the National Medal of the Arts from President Barack Obama in 2010.

Rollins was celebrated for his improvisational mastery and prolific output of more than 60 albums as a bandleader across a career spanning more than six decades. He is survived by a legacy that shaped the course of modern jazz.
